title: Mesoamerica, Olmecs to Aztecs
tagline: From the Olmec heartland to Tenochtitlan's fall: the cities and states of Mexico and Central America.
intro: From about 1200 BCE, when the Olmecs built San Lorenzo on Mexico's Gulf Coast, to the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521, the peoples of Mesoamerica raised cities, carved monuments to their rulers and fought for tribute. Olmec images of rulers and gods helped shape the art of later peoples such as the Maya, and Teotihuacan's influence reached as far as the Maya cities of Tikal and Copán. The Maya never formed a single state, and after the southern kingdoms emptied, Chichén Itzá led the north, while the Aztecs looked back to the Toltecs of Tula. The last stops show the Aztec Triple Alliance and two neighbours that held out against it, the Purépecha and Tlaxcala.

steps.why: The Olmecs built the first great centres of Mesoamerica, San Lorenzo and then La Venta, in the lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast between about 1200 and 400 BCE.
Seventeen basalt heads up to 3.4 metres high, thought to be portraits of rulers, carved from stone brought from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas by means still unknown.
The Maya built hundreds of cities but never a single state, and their scribes created the most complete writing system of the ancient Americas.
A planned city of perhaps 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, whose pyramids and architecture influenced Mesoamerica as far as the Maya cities of Tikal and Copán.
Sacked by Calakmul in 599 and 611, this Maya city was rebuilt under K'inich Janaab' Pakal, whose tomb was found in the Temple of the Inscriptions in 1952.
In the 10th century this Yucatán city rose to be a regional capital of the northern Maya, its buildings mixing central Mexican styles with those of the region.
Tula's warrior statues and colonnaded halls have close parallels at Chichén Itzá, and the Aztecs later revered the Toltecs as the founders of civilisation.
From 1428 the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan ruled central Mexico through tribute, from an island city of 200,000 or more people.
Ruled from Tzintzuntzan on Lake Pátzcuaro, this western kingdom routed Axayacatl's Aztec army in the late 1470s and led Mesoamerica in copper and bronze.
Four Nahua city-states that resisted the Triple Alliance for generations, then allied with Hernán Cortés in 1519 and helped take Tenochtitlan in 1521.

title: Civilisations of the Andes
tagline: From Caral's platform mounds to the last Inca stronghold at Vilcabamba, the civilisations of the Andes.
intro: Caral–Supe, on Peru's north-central coast, raised platform mounds from about 3000 BCE and is the oldest known civilisation of the Americas. Later Andean peoples built on what came before: Chavín's temple cult spread across the central Andes, Paracas is believed to have evolved into the Nazca culture, and Wari's roads and cord records foreshadowed the institutions of the Incas. The stops move between the desert coast, where Moche lords and the kings of Chimor ruled irrigated valleys, and the highlands of Wari and Tiwanaku. They end with Tawantinsuyu, which stretched some 4,000 km along the Andes, and the Neo-Inca State that held out at Vilcabamba until 1572.

steps.why: As many as thirty centres in three small coastal valleys raised stepped platform mounds and sunken plazas from about 3000 BCE, with no pottery and no evidence of warfare.
A highland temple town of c. 950–400 BCE whose priests drew pilgrims from coast, mountains and forest, and whose art of jaguars, eagles and caimans spread far across Peru.
On Peru's south coast its dead were wrapped in layers of embroidered cloth, the Paracas Necropolis textiles, among the finest of the Pre-Columbian Andes.
Figures and lines scraped into the desert between the Nazca and Palpa valleys, mostly between about 500 BCE and 500 CE, by the Paracas and Nazca cultures.
On Peru's north coast, c. 100–800 CE, lords ruled irrigated valleys from adobe platforms such as the Huaca del Sol, and potters made lifelike portrait vessels.
Often called the first Andean empire, Wari planted planned centres across highland Peru from about 600, and its roads and cord records foreshadowed the Incas.
A ceremonial city at about 3,850 metres near Lake Titicaca, sustained by raised fields and llama caravans, whose Staff God imagery spread across the southern Andes.
The Chimú capital near Trujillo, the largest adobe city of the pre-Columbian Americas, with some ten walled royal compounds; the Incas took it around 1470.
Tawantinsuyu stretched some 4,000 km and ran on labour tribute, storehouses, a 40,000 km road network and khipu records, until Pizarro's conquest in 1532–1533.
Founded by Manco Inca in 1537, it kept the Inca court and Sun cult alive at Vilcabamba until Spanish forces took it and executed Túpac Amaru in 1572.

title: West Africa's Golden Age
tagline: The empires that grew rich on the Saharan gold and salt trade, and their southern neighbours.
intro: Caravan routes across the Sahara carried gold, slaves and ivory north and salt, horses and textiles south, and with them came Islam and literacy. Ghana, Mali and Songhai grew rich on that trade, and under Mali and Songhai Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning whose scholars were famous across the Islamic world. Further east, Kanem-Bornu tied the Lake Chad basin to the route to Tripoli, and the walled Hausa city-kingdoms linked the Sahara with the forest. To the south, Benin's royal guilds cast the Benin Bronzes, Oyo's cavalry made it the leading power between the Niger and the Volta, and the Asante were bound together by the Golden Stool.

steps.why: Caravans carried gold, slaves and ivory north across the Sahara and salt, horses and textiles south, and this trade underpinned the wealth of Ghana, Mali and Songhai.
Widely identified as the capital of the Ghana Empire, a twin city of a Muslim merchant quarter and a royal town, and a major centre of the gold and salt trade.
Founded by Sundiata Keita, Mali sent the gold of Bambuk and Bure into the Saharan trade, and in 1324 Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca dazzled Cairo with it.
A city near the Niger at the southern edge of the Sahara, a centre of trade and Islamic learning under Mali that reached its height under Songhai.
The largest empire in West African history held Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné on the Niger Bend, until a Moroccan army with firearms routed it at Tondibi in 1591.
Ruled for close to eight centuries by the Sayfawa dynasty, this Lake Chad empire held the route to Tripoli and tied the central Sudan to the Muslim world.
Walled city-kingdoms such as Kano, Katsina and Zazzau never united, but shared a language, court institutions and a trade network linking the Sahara and the forest.
From Benin City the Edo Obas built a regional empire from the 15th century, and royal guilds cast the Benin Bronzes, looted by a British expedition in 1897.
Its cavalry made this Yoruba savannah state the leading power between the Niger and the Volta, and in the 18th century it forced Dahomey into vassalage.
The sacred throne of the Asante, believed to hold the soul of the nation; the British governor's demand of 1900 that it be surrendered provoked a war.

title: East and Southern Africa
tagline: Highland Christian kings, Swahili merchant towns, plateau gold and the kingdoms that faced Portugal and Britain.
intro: Aksum, in highland Ethiopia and Eritrea, grew rich on the Red Sea trade and under King Ezana became one of the first states to adopt Christianity. On the coast, Swahili merchant towns traded across the Indian Ocean from around the 8th century, and island Kilwa controlled the gold trade from Sofala. That gold came from the interior, where Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa Empire rose one after another. The last stops turn to kingdoms that fought European expansion: Kongo and Ndongo against Portugal, and the Zulu Kingdom, which routed a British force at Isandlwana in 1879.

steps.why: Aksum grew rich trading ivory and gold through its Red Sea port of Adulis, and under King Ezana became one of the first states to adopt Christianity.
Medieval churches carved out of the rock in the northern Ethiopian highlands, linked with King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty and still a major site of pilgrimage.
The Bantu speech of the East African coast took shape in merchant towns that traded across the Indian Ocean from around the 8th century, absorbing many Arabic words.
Seat of the Kilwa Sultanate, which controlled the gold trade from Sofala; Ibn Battuta praised it in 1331, and the Portuguese sacked it in 1505.
Around 1220 its rulers moved onto a hill above the Limpopo, apart from the commoners below, and were buried with gold, among it the famous gold-foil rhinoceros.
A Shona kingdom rich on cattle and on gold and ivory sent to Sofala, whose dry-stone walls are the largest precolonial stone structures in southern Africa.
Founded around 1430 as Great Zimbabwe declined, this Shona state between the Zambezi and Limpopo traded its gold through Swahili and later Portuguese merchants.
Ruled from Mbanza Kongo, it adopted Christianity and Portuguese literacy, and in 1526 Afonso I wrote to Portugal protesting the abuses of the slave trade.
Queen of the Mbundu kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba, she allied with the Dutch in the 1640s and resisted Portuguese expansion for decades, making peace in 1656.
Shaka turned a small chiefdom into the strongest state in southeastern Africa from 1816, and in 1879 the Zulu routed a British force at Isandlwana.
